done.why: I got the coal into the basket and lowered it, then squeezed through the timber slot, but the far side is pitch dark. The shaft text makes clear I need a second light to send down, and I don't have one. Getting one meant crossing the coal-mine maze again and getting past a bat I have no garlic for, since my sack was scattered when I died. I'd read everything nearby closely, the maze had worn me out, and this felt like an honest place to stop.

about: It's the old white house and the empire under it, with the familiar rooms and treasures, but the objects talk back more than I remember. A sword has "been in worse places than a living room." A trophy case "expects to be filled." A pile of coal hints at what it could become. The part I spent longest in is the coal mine: a shaft, a basket and a timber slot, with careful sentences telling you exactly what will fit and what light goes where.

moments.note: The sword description is dry and charming. 'Plainly been in worse places than a living room.'
The gothic lettering translates to 'This space intentionally left blank.' I laughed.
'The patient air of something that expects to be filled.' The trophy case has a personality.
'go upstairs' isn't understood. Plain 'up' works.
The troll description is the best writing so far: 'watching you the way a cook watches a chicken.'
I disarmed the troll and he begged for his life. I tried to spare him, but 'spare' isn't a word it knows.
'Your load is too heavy, the sword not least of it.' Even the refusal is written well.
The troll took my head off. Some of that was my own fault, since I sent several attacks without reading between them.
The death text is wonderful: 'somebody tidy has put the lamp back in the living room.'
The chasm: 'a dark that your lamp does not so much light as annoy.' My favourite line.
The painting gets a tender description: 'hard to look at it for long, and harder to look away.'
The chimney refusal lists exactly what I'm carrying and what would fit. Clear and in character.
The sword turned up outside with the 'plain things', not in a dark corner. That was a small surprise after the death message.
The railing description quietly hints at tying a rope and is lovely to read: 'the most reassuring thing you have seen in some time.' I'd left my rope in the studio, though.
The bat carried me off. I had no garlic because my sack was lost when I died.
The coal hints at becoming something else without saying it outright.
The timber-slot refusal names exactly which items won't go through. Very helpful.
The coal mine maze: every room is 'a nondescript part of a coal mine.' Dropping coal as a marker helped a little, but mapping it was a chore.
The shaft description spells out the light puzzle in prose that is plain and still graceful: 'a light that goes down in the basket stays down with it.'
The bat grabbed me again and dropped me back in the maze.
Through the slot it was pitch black, and 'feel around' didn't do anything.

wished: To spare the disarmed troll when he begged for his life.
To feel my way around in the dark room past the timber slot.
For 'go upstairs' to work, not just 'up'.
For coal-mine rooms to have even one small detail each, so the maze could be read and not only mapped.
To find out where my brown sack went after I died.

lines.line: It is very old, and has plainly been in worse places than a living room.
lines.why: It set the dry, affectionate tone of the whole place.

lines.line: It has the patient air of something that expects to be filled.
lines.why: It turns the scoring goal into a character.

lines.line: He is watching you the way a cook watches a chicken.
lines.why: Menace and comedy in one line.

lines.line: and somebody tidy has put the lamp back in the living room.
lines.why: A death message that made me smile when I could have been annoyed.

lines.line: a dark that your lamp does not so much light as annoy. A pebble kicked over the edge is never heard from again. Neither, by the look of it, was whoever kicked the last one.
lines.why: The best sentence I read here.

lines.line: done with such tenderness that it is hard to look at it for long, and harder to look away.
lines.why: A treasure written as something worth looking at, not just loot.

lines.line: It is the most reassuring thing you have seen in some time.
lines.why: A hint written as character, not as an instruction.

lines.line: a light that goes down in the basket stays down with it, and is not up here with you.
lines.why: It explains the puzzle cleanly without breaking the voice.

fun.why: The house, the gallery and the chimney were a pleasure, and so was the troll's description. Dying to the troll, getting carried off by the bat twice, and the nondescript coal-mine maze drained the fun in the second half.

engagement.why: I kept examining everything because the examine text kept paying off. Only the maze made me want to stop.

difficulty.why: Losing the sack (and its garlic) on death made the bat a real wall. The maze takes trial and error, and the shaft needs a second light I couldn't easily get. The refusal messages are fair and clear, but the puzzles stacked on top of each other.

interestingness.why: Familiar ground, but the new descriptions give it fresh texture. Where things went after my death was a nice wrinkle. The shaft and slot puzzle is laid out unusually clearly.

prose.why: Even the refusals are written with care. The chasm, the troll, the painting, the railing and the shaft are all sharp, funny and precise. The original's sparse coal-mine rooms stand out against all that.
